summary: This comprehensive module covers the engineering principles, system layouts, operational components, and environmental considerations of both Hydroelectric Power Plants and Nuclear Power Plants. In Part I (Hydroelectric), it details hydrology concepts including mass curves (Rippl's diagram, 1 second-metre month = 2592 × 10³ m³) for reservoir storage capacity determination, site selection criteria, and the complete plant layout comprising catchment area, dam, reservoir, forebay, spillways, high-pressure penstocks, surge tanks (water hammer mitigation), hydraulic turbines (Pelton, Francis, Kaplan), and synchronous alternators. In Part II (Nuclear), it explores the physics of nuclear fission, energy release (200 MeV per fission event, where 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; 1 kg of U²³⁵ yields 25 × 10⁶ kWh of heat energy, equivalent to burning 2,500 tonnes of high-grade coal, developing 6.5 × 10⁶ kWh of electricity), and the architecture of nuclear reactors with their seven essential components: (a) Fuel (U²³⁸₉₂, Th²³²₉₀, U²³⁵₉₂), (b) Moderator (D₂O, carbon/graphite), (c) Reflector, (d) Control rods (boron), (e) Coolant (gaseous CO₂, liquid D₂O, liquid sodium), (f) Shielding (absorbing α, β particles, γ rays), and (g) Structure. Finally, it contrasts the economic, technical, and operational characteristics of hydro, nuclear, and conventional thermal/diesel generation.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is a Mass Curve, and how is the required storage capacity of a hydroelectric reservoir determined from it?
sa.a:
A Mass Curve is a graphical representation of the cumulative volume of river water inflow (where 1 second-metre month = 2592 × 10³ m³) plotted against time (months of the year). The slope of the curve at any point indicates the rate of inflow (discharge).

To find the reservoir storage capacity:
(i) Trough points (low-inflow dry periods) are identified on the curve (points B and C), and a tangent line RS is drawn touching them, representing the required uniform discharge rate.
(ii) A parallel tangent AX is drawn touching the peak point A of the mass curve.
(iii) The maximum vertical distance between AX and RS gives the minimum reservoir storage capacity required to maintain firm power output.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State any four major merits of a Hydroelectric Power Plant.
sa.a:
Four major merits of a hydroelectric station are:
(i) Zero Fuel Cost: No fuel is required by a hydropower station; it utilizes naturally flowing water.
(ii) Neat and Clean: It is a very neat and clean plant with zero smoke, greenhouse emissions, or ash disposal problems.
(iii) Cheap O&M Costs & Long Life: Operation and maintenance costs are very cheap; plant life is long (50 to 100+ years) and efficiency does not decrease with age.
(iv) Rapid Starting & Load Variation: Load can be varied quickly and rapidly; the plant can be run up and synchronised very quickly with no standby losses.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Explain the purpose and functioning of a Surge Tank in a hydroelectric power station.
sa.a:
A surge tank is a small reservoir or vertical tank open at the top, installed on the penstock between the dam and power house to protect against 'water hammer':
(i) When the load on the generator is reduced, the governor tends to close the turbine gates, causing water pressure to increase rapidly in the penstock. The surge tank absorbs the rejected water and the water level rises, relieving pressure variation and preventing penstock rupture.
(ii) When a larger load is demanded, the gate opens to allow a large quantity of water to flow. The surge tank supplies immediate water to prevent the tendency of a vacuum or negative pressure in the penstock.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Classify hydrodynamic machines (hydraulic turbines) based on the type of flow of water.
sa.a:
According to the type of flow of water, hydrodynamic machines (hydraulic turbines) are classified as follows:
(i) Axis along the shaft of machine — Axial flow turbines (Propeller turbine and Kaplan turbine).
(ii) Axis along the radius — Radial flow turbines (Francis turbine).
(iii) Axis along the tangential directions — Tangential flow turbines (Pelton wheel).
(iv) Mixed flow (Radial inlet and axial outlet) — Francis turbine.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Differentiate between an Earth Dam and a Gravity Dam used in hydroelectric schemes.
sa.a:
(i) Earth Dam: Classified according to structural materials; constructed of compacted earth, sand, and gravel with a central concrete core wall. Used up to about 100 m height for pervious foundations. Protected by stone pitching at the water line against wave erosion and vegetation against rain erosion. Seepage loss is higher than other dams.

(ii) Solid Gravity Dam: A massive masonry or concrete structure built on solid bed rock. Resists the immense overturning and sliding forces of impounded head water solely by its own enormous self-weight.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the fundamental constituents of a complete Nuclear Power Plant.
sa.a:
The constituents of a nuclear power plant are as follows:
(i) Nuclear reactor (generates heat through controlled nuclear fission)
(ii) Heat exchanger / Steam generator (transfers fission heat from reactor coolant to feed water)
(iii) Steam turbine (converts steam thermal energy into shaft rotational mechanical power)
(iv) Condenser (condenses exhaust steam into water using circulating cooling water)
(v) Alternator (synchronous generator that converts shaft mechanical power into electrical energy).

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What is Nuclear Fission? State the energy released by the fission of 1 kg of Uranium-235.
sa.a:
Nuclear Fission is the process in which the nucleus of a heavy atom (such as U²³⁵₉₂, Th²³²₉₀, or Pu²³⁹₉₄) is bombarded by a thermal neutron and splits into two lighter nuclei of lower atomic weight (such as barium and krypton), accompanied by the release of 2 to 3 fast neutrons (at a speed of 2 × 10⁷ m/s) and an immense amount of energy (~200 MeV per fission, where 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J).

Energy Equivalent: The complete fission of 1 kg of Uranium-235 (U²³⁵) yields approximately 25 × 10⁶ kWh of heat energy, which is equivalent to burning about 2,500 tonnes of high-grade coal. About 6.5 × 10⁶ kWh of electrical energy is developed from 1 kg of uranium.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): Explain the function of a Moderator in a nuclear reactor and state the desirable properties of a good moderator.
sa.a:
Objective of Moderator: To reduce the speed of fast neutrons emitted during fission (from ~2 × 10⁷ m/s down to thermal speeds). When fast neutrons collide with the nuclei of moderator material of equal mass, they lose energy through elastic collisions without being captured.

A good moderator should have the following properties:
(i) High scattering cross-section.
(ii) Low neutron absorption cross-section.
Common Materials: Hydrogen, deuterium, helium, lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon (graphite), nitrogen, and oxygen. Heavy water (D₂O) is an ideal moderating material.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): What are Control Rods? Name the materials used and explain how they regulate reactor power.
sa.a:
Objective of Control Rods: To regulate the fissioning in the reactor by absorbing excess neutrons. They are generally made of Boron (or Cadmium) and are inserted into the reactor core from the top of the reactor vessel.

Regulation Mechanism:
(i) If the fissioning rate is to be increased, the control rods are moved out slightly so that a lesser number of neutrons will be absorbed by them.
(ii) To reduce the fissioning rate, the control rods are moved slightly in to absorb more neutrons.

sa.q: Part A (3 Marks): State the critical factors governing the selection of site for a Nuclear Power Plant.
sa.a:
The factors to be considered for selecting a nuclear power plant site are:
(i) Proximity to Water Body: The site should be selected near a river, lake, or seaside for abundant cooling water.
(ii) Safety Distance: A reasonable distance between the nuclear power plant and the nearest populated area to mitigate radioactivity dangers in the atmosphere.
(iii) Transportation: Adequate transportation facilities are required during the construction stage for heavy reactor vessels.
(iv) Load Centre: Plants should be located as near to the load centre as possible to reduce transmission costs.
(v) Waste Disposal: Adequate space for safe disposal of radioactive waste.
(vi) Ground Supporting Strength: The land should have the supporting strength to carry reactors having a weight of 1,00,000 tonnes and impose a bearing pressure of 50 tonnes/m².

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of a neat schematic diagram, explain the general layout and major components of a Hydroelectric Power Plant from catchment area to tail race. (8 marks)
(b) Describe the functions of the Forebay, Spillway, and Penstock in a hydro station. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) General Layout and Components of a Hydroelectric Power Plant:

The schematic arrangement and flow sequence comprises:
(i) Catchment Area & Reservoir: Rainfall runoff collects in the catchment area and is impounded in the reservoir behind the dam.
(ii) Dam and Head Works: Built across the river to store water and create the necessary head of water.
(iii) Pressure Tunnel & Forebay: Water flows through a pressure tunnel and intake gate to the forebay.
(iv) Penstock & Surge Tank: Water enters the penstock (closed conduit). A surge tank is installed on the penstock to relieve water hammer pressure variations.
(v) Inlet Valve & Hydraulic Turbine: High-pressure water passes the inlet valve and enters the turbine, causing the runner to rotate by hydrodynamic action.
(vi) Alternator (Generator): Directly coupled to the turbine shaft; converts mechanical power into 3-phase electrical energy.
(vii) Switchgear & Transmission Line: Generated voltage is switched, stepped up, and transmitted through high-voltage transmission lines.
(viii) Tail Race: Spent water discharging from the turbine flows through the draft tube into the tail race back to the river.

(b) Functions of Forebay, Spillway, and Penstock:
(i) Forebay: An enlarged body of water just above the intake for storing water temporarily to meet hourly load fluctuations (either a pond behind the diversion dam or an enlarged section of a canal).
(ii) Spillway: Acts as a safety valve. It discharges the overflow of water to the downstream side when the reservoir is full, mainly during flood periods. Classified into: (a) Spillway dams or overflow spillways, (b) Chute spillways, (c) Side channel spillways, (d) Shaft spillways, and (e) Siphon spillways.
(iii) Penstock: A closed conduit which connects the forebay or surge tank to the scroll case of the hydraulic turbine.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Explain the construction and functioning of a Surge Tank with a neat diagram. Discuss the phenomenon of water hammer and how the surge tank mitigates it. (8 marks)
(b) Classify hydrodynamic machines (hydraulic turbines) according to the type of flow of water, providing practical examples. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Surge Tank Construction, Water Hammer, and Working:

1. The Phenomenon of Water Hammer:
- When the load on the generator is reduced, the governor tends to close the turbine gates, rapidly stopping the moving column of water.
- This sudden deceleration increases water pressure abruptly inside the penstock, causing a severe hydraulic shock wave termed 'water hammering' that can burst the penstock.
- Conversely, during sudden load increase, the gate opens to allow large quantities of water to flow, creating a tendency of vacuum or negative pressure that can cause penstock walls to buckle inward.

2. Construction and Functioning of Surge Tank:
- A surge tank is a small reservoir or vertical cylinder open at the top, placed on the closed conduit penstock near the power station.
- Operation during Load Rejection: When turbine gates close, the rejected water rises in the surge tank. This controls the pressure variation and absorbs the momentum, preventing water hammer damage.
- Operation during Load Demand: The water level in the surge tank falls to immediately supply the required flow while water in the pressure tunnel accelerates, preventing negative pressure.

(b) Classification of Hydrodynamic Machines (Hydraulic Turbines):
According to the type of flow of water, hydraulic turbines are classified as follows:
(i) Axis along the shaft of machine — Axial flow turbines (Propeller turbine and Kaplan turbine).
(ii) Axis along the radius — Radial flow turbines (Francis turbine).
(iii) Axis along the tangential directions — Tangential flow turbines (Pelton wheel).
(iv) Mixed flow (Radial inlet and axial outlet) — Francis turbine.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) With the aid of a neat schematic diagram, explain the constituents and working of a complete Nuclear Power Plant. (8 marks)
(b) Describe the functions of: (i) Moderator, (ii) Control Rods, (iii) Thermal Shielding, and (iv) Coolants in a nuclear reactor. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Constituents and Working of a Nuclear Power Plant:

The constituents of a nuclear power plant are:
(i) Nuclear Reactor: Contains fuel blocks where controlled nuclear fission generates heat.
(ii) Heat Exchanger / Steam Generator: Hot fluid from the reactor circulates through heat exchanging tubes, transferring heat to feed water to generate high-pressure steam.
(iii) Steam Turbine: High-pressure steam expands through turbine blades, converting thermal energy into rotational mechanical power.
(iv) Surface Condenser: Exhaust steam from the turbine is condensed back to water by circulating cold river water.
(v) Alternator: Synchronous machine directly coupled to the steam turbine, converting mechanical power into electrical power dispatched to the bus bar.

(b) Operational Functions of Core Components:
(i) Moderator: Reduces fast neutron velocity (~2 × 10⁷ m/s down to thermal speeds) through elastic collisions with light nuclei (heavy water D₂O, graphite, beryllium), enabling sustained chain reaction.
(ii) Control Rods: Regulate fissioning rate by absorbing excess neutrons. Made of boron and inserted into the core from the top. Moving them out increases the reaction; inserting them deeper reduces or shuts down fissioning.
(iii) Thermal Shielding: Surrounds the reactor core and absorbs radiations in the form of α, β particles, γ rays and escaping neutrons. Constructed from iron, with coolant flowing over it to carry away absorbed heat.
(iv) Coolant: Medium through which heat developed in the reactor is transferred to the heat exchanger for power generation. Types used:
  • Gases: Air, helium, hydrogen, and CO₂.
  • Liquids: Light and heavy water (D₂O).
  • Metals: Molten sodium and lithium.

essay.q:
Part B (12 Marks): (a) Describe the seven main components of a nuclear reactor with their engineering functions. (8 marks)
(b) State the merits and demerits of Nuclear Power Plants compared to other generating stations. (4 marks)
essay.a:
(a) Seven Main Components of a Nuclear Reactor:

A nuclear reactor consists of the following seven components:
(i) Fuel: Natural uranium consisting of 99.23% of U²³⁸₉₂, 0.71% of U²³⁵₉₂, and 0.06% of U²³⁴₉₂; enriched with U²³⁵₉₂ along with aluminium or zirconium for dilution. Fission of 1 kg of U²³⁵ yields 25 × 10⁶ kWh of heat energy (≈ 2,500 tonnes of coal) and 6.5 × 10⁶ kWh of electricity.
(ii) Moderator: Slows down fast neutrons by elastic collisions; requires high scattering cross-section and low absorption cross-section (D₂O, carbon/graphite).
(iii) Reflector: Surrounds the reactor core within thermal shielding to bounce escaping neutrons back into the core, reducing their speed to aid the chain reaction.
(iv) Control: Boron control rods inserted from the top to regulate fission rate by absorbing excess neutrons.
(v) Coolant: Transfers heat developed in the reactor to the heat exchanger (CO₂ gas, D₂O liquid, molten sodium metal).
(vi) Shielding: Inner iron thermal shield absorbing α, β particles, γ rays and escaping neutrons, enclosed by heavy concrete biological shield.
(vii) Structure: Structural containment vessel housing core components.

(b) Merits and Demerits of Nuclear Power Plants:

Merits:
(i) The amount of fuel required is quite small; hence there is no problem of bulk fuel transportation.
(ii) Requires less land area compared to hydro or solar plants of the same size.
(iii) Produces valuable fissile material (plutonium) extracted when fuel is renewed.
(iv) Can be located near load centres, reducing primary power distribution costs.
(v) Most economical in case of large capacity; vast world nuclear fuel reserves can run for thousands of years.
(vi) Control of power output is extremely flexible.

Demerits:
(i) Initial capital cost is very high.
(ii) Technical knowledge and specially trained personnel are required for erection, commissioning, and maintenance.
(iii) Dangerous radioactive pollution risks in the atmosphere in case of accidents.
(iv) Not well suited for varying loads (best operated at steady baseload).
(v) Fuel is expensive and difficult to recover.
(vi) Disposal of radioactive waste products is a major problem.
